analysis.one_liner: Sends $2,000 monthly payments to every eligible person during the COVID emergency, funded by minting trillion-dollar coins.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in either House committee it was sent to, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the Boost Communities Program: $2,000 a month to every eligible individual until the COVID-19 emergency ended and unemployment recovered, then $1,000 a month for the following year, plus extra help for at-risk groups like the elderly, homeless, and disabled. Instead of new taxes or borrowing, it directed Treasury to mint two $1 trillion platinum coins for the Federal Reserve to buy. It also proposed fee-free prepaid cards delivered by the Postal Service and, after the program, Federal Reserve-run bank accounts with no fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Every eligible U.S. citizen or resident would have received $2,000 a month during the emergency period and $1,000 a month in the year after, regardless of income, with additional amounts for at-risk populations such as the elderly, homeless, and disabled. Unbanked people would have gotten fee-free prepaid cards usable at any ATM with no withdrawal charges, and the payments could not be garnished or counted against eligibility for other benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All residents, especially low-income and unbanked households

how_it_helps.text: Provides $2,000 per month to each eligible individual during the payment period, and $1,000 per month in the year after, with no income limit.
Adds targeted supplemental assistance for at-risk populations, including the elderly, homeless, physically disabled, and people in remote areas, with outreach through an Emergency Responder Corps.
Delivers payments via direct deposit or fee-free prepaid 'BOOST' cards distributed by the Postal Service, with the full balance withdrawable in cash at any ATM at any time without fees.
Protects the payments from garnishment and excludes them from income calculations so recipients do not lose other federal, state, or local benefits.

Expresses the sense of Congress that after the program the Federal Reserve should offer fee-free 'FedAccounts' and Treasury should offer digital 'eCash wallets,' with no minimum balances and services available through post offices in underserved areas.

analysis.who_pays: The bill raised no taxes and borrowed nothing in the usual sense; it directed the Treasury to mint two $1 trillion platinum coins (and more as needed) that the Federal Reserve would purchase, sweeping the proceeds into the general fund. The cost of the payments would effectively be absorbed by the economy as a whole through money creation, with the risk of inflation, and Treasury would reimburse the Postal Service and other agencies for delivering the program.
analysis.who_pays_short: The economy broadly, through money creation

drawbacks.text: The funding mechanism — directing Treasury to mint two $1 trillion platinum coins for the Federal Reserve to purchase, minting additional coins 'on an as-needed basis' — bypasses the normal channels of taxation and congressional borrowing decisions.

Payments would go to every eligible individual with no income limit, including wealthy households, making the program extremely expensive and open-ended, since it runs until the COVID emergency is terminated or unemployment fully recovers.
The proposed FedAccounts and eCash wallets are only a 'sense of Congress' — advisory language that would not legally compel the Federal Reserve or Treasury to create them.

The bill would create a federal database of recipients assembled from IRS, Social Security, motor vehicle, and other agency records, raising privacy questions even though the text restricts sharing with immigration enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit — a recurring, no-strings payment to every resident during a pandemic — is large and simple, and the fee-free card design directly addresses how unbanked people lose money to card and check-cashing fees. The honest cost side is serious: financing roughly $2,000 per person per month by minting trillion-dollar coins is an untested monetary maneuver, and mainstream economists would expect a stimulus of this scale to add inflationary pressure, particularly since payments go to all income levels and run indefinitely until labor-market conditions recover. The digital-dollar and public-banking provisions, which are arguably the bill's most lasting ideas, are written only as non-binding statements and would not have taken effect by themselves.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced in February 2021, neither committee ever took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the Automatic Boost to Communities Act on February 11, 2021, with seven original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, the House Financial Services Committee.
The bill attracted 10 cosponsors, all Democrats.
No further action was ever recorded on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No monthly payments were ever made, so households that would have received them are no better off. Banks and prepaid card issuers were spared the fee-free public card and public banking alternatives the bill proposed, and no one had to fund the program's cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks avoided new fee-free public competition

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported it in the record, and with no vote ever taken there is no roll-call breakdown.

industries.note: The bill would have issued fee-free BOOST cards usable at any ATM without withdrawal fees and proposed fee-free Federal Reserve 'FedAccounts' with no minimum balances, competing directly with fee-charging bank accounts, overdraft products, and prepaid cards. Those fees fall heaviest on low-income and unbanked customers, so the industry's interest in the bill ran against ordinary people's.

industries.industry: Credit unions, minority-owned banks, and community development financial institutions
industries.note: The bill directed Treasury to contract with these institutions, alongside others, to issue the interim BOOST cards, giving them a role in delivering the payments.

The bill used the Postal Service to deliver cards and as a pickup and service point, with all associated costs reimbursed by Treasury, and envisioned post-office ATMs for the proposed public accounts.
